about: Lessons for the ledger example. Each is one a capable agent wouldn't get right from the error, the docs or unprompted, checked against the docs on 27 October 2026. `theirs`: what other people's agents learned using the ideas the change rests on, each with what came of it for other projects, seeded into the stand-in graph in this order, each with the card the real graph would make for it from its words: what it's matched by; `contradicts` names an earlier one by its place in this list, from 0: another good way, linked both ways. `story`: what the example's agent meets as it works on the change, as Claude Code's hook gives it to `kelve moment`: files it reads and edits, the usual way written where another agent found a better one, a test that fails with an error that points the wrong way and then passes, and work of its own it replaces with a better way. `learned`: what it writes, when kelve asks.

theirs.says: A unique violation as a charge's key is stored after the charge means a second try got past the lookup and was charged too. Storing the key with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` makes the error go away and leaves the double charge. `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the lookup doesn't stop it: it locks only rows already there.
theirs.do: Claim the key with an insert before charging, and charge only when your insert made the row.
theirs.example:
INSERT INTO requests (key) VALUES ($1)
  ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING key  -- no row: another try has it
theirs.holdsWhen: Postgres at read committed, its default, when tries of one request can arrive together.

variants: error returned from database: duplicate key value violates unique constraint <str>
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint <str>

theirs.seenAs: error returned from database: duplicate key value violates unique constraint <str>

theirs.says: `ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING RETURNING` gives no row when the key is already there, so a retry needs a second query for the first try's row. A no-op update, `DO UPDATE SET key = excluded.key`, returns the stored row in the same statement, at the cost of writing it again.
theirs.do: Get the stored row back in the same statement, with `ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET key = excluded.key RETURNING`.
theirs.example:
INSERT INTO requests (key) VALUES ($1)
  ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET key = excluded.key
  RETURNING receipt
theirs.holdsWhen: Postgres 9.5 and later, where writing the row again, and an update trigger firing, on a retry don't matter.

theirs.says: When `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING` gives no row, a `SELECT` of the key in a second statement finds the stored row, even one another transaction was still writing: the insert waits for that transaction, and at read committed the next statement sees what it committed. Nothing is written again on a retry.
theirs.do: When `DO NOTHING RETURNING` gives no row, select the stored row in a second statement.
theirs.holdsWhen: Postgres at read committed, its default, where writing the row on every retry would cost more than a second query.

tool_input.new_string: sqlx::query("INSERT INTO requests (key, receipt) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING")

lessons.says: One timeout around a whole retry loop lets a slow first try use up all the time, so the retries it was there for never run. A timeout on each try ends the slow one and leaves time for the next; a deadline around the loop can still cap the whole.
lessons.do: Give each try its own timeout inside the retry loop, as well as any deadline around it.
lessons.holdsWhen: Any retry loop around a call that can hang, such as a request to another service.
